claims.claim: Writers are told not to rely on internet searches, wikis, or prior-edition products for setting facts.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: Tone is gated by a Lord of the Rings / Game of Thrones plausibility test; humor and tragedy are allowed only if they do not overtake the general tone.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: ring wraiths aren’t used for gags

claims.claim: D&D's brand voice frames adventure as a team's story rather than a lone knight's.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Teamwork and friendship are a huge part

claims.claim: Gender-neutral wording is expected whenever a person's gender is unknown or irrelevant, and the reader's gender is not assumed.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: gender neutrality whenever the gender of a person is unknown

claims.claim: Rules text achieves gender neutrality chiefly by being written in the second person.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: writing in the second person whenever possible

claims.claim: v1.08a newly permits singular 'they/their' but tells writers to reach for it only when no other pleasing alternative exists.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: 'He or she' is to be used sparingly; 'he/she' and 's/he' are banned; alternating he and she for inclusivity is banned.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: In 2019 'man' and 'woman' were reserved for humans only, so a dwarf is a 'male dwarf', never a 'dwarf man'.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: Editorial rules such as the man/woman restriction may be broken in dialogue and first-person narrative, because a character need not follow house style.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: This rule can be broken in dialogue and first-person narrative

claims.claim: Gendered suffixes are avoided ('priest', 'actor'); 'priestess'/'actress' survive only inside an in-world title or organization name.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: Deities are called 'god' regardless of gender in editorial voice; 'goddess' is reserved for in-world usage.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: use “god” whether the deity is male or female

claims.claim: Headings descend Chapter Title > Heading 1 > 2 > 3 > Inline Subhead without skipping, and exist for structure, never aesthetics.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Use a heading for a structural reason, not an aesthetic one

claims.claim: The inline subhead (heading 4) is set in bold italics and ends with a period, exclamation point, or question mark, not a colon.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: should be followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

claims.claim: Bold is the only emphasis device, and a term already in the section heading gets no emphasis in running text.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: Sidebars are rationed; any sidebar that must follow a specific passage to make sense should be folded into body text instead.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: The best sidebars can appear anywhere on a page
